Countries became deadlocked over whether the cover decision would reiterate the call to transition away from fossil fuels and concerns that it promoted overreliance on carbon capture and storage. There was also frustration that negotiators could not agree on a specific dollar [...] “The hollow outcome at COP31 was a failure of political leadership, not a failure of the Paris Agreement. plan.title: COP31 in Antalya: Talks Collapse, What Happens Next
plan.description: COP31 in Antalya ended on 22 November 2026 without its main political deal, the Antalya Pact, though several negotiation items and Action Agenda results did succeed. This video covers what was agreed, what failed, and what experts say comes next.

beats.narration: Two weeks of climate talks. Almost fifty hours of overtime. And still no deal. The longest COP ever ended in Antalya with the world's main political decision left on the table.

props.title: COP31: The Longest Climate Talks Ever
props.subtitle: Antalya, Türkiye, November 2026

beats.narration: COP31 President Murat Kurum closed the session at 7:33 pm on Sunday, 22 November. He said he was leaving the deadlock to the judgment of the entire world and humanity.

props.text: I leave the deadlock of the negotiations to the judgement of the entire world and humanity.

beats.narration: The package was called the Antalya Pact. It had two cover decisions. Kurum admitted there was no consensus, saying some parties in the hall opposed the text.

props.definition: The proposed pair of cover decisions, under the COP and the Paris Agreement body, that COP31 failed to adopt.
props.example: Rejected at the closing plenary, 22 November 2026

beats.narration: Why did it fail? Countries split over whether to repeat the call to transition away from fossil fuels. There was also no agreed dollar finance figure. And the mitigation work programme was rejected too.
The European Union formally objected, saying the text failed to meet the moment. Panama also rejected it, arguing that governments must not negotiate the minimum threshold, but act.
Yet not everything failed. According to UN Climate Change, almost 200 nations agreed on a Just Transition and on items covering finance, adaptation, technology and transparency.

The Action Agenda delivered real-economy progress. The European Investment Bank targets over 30 billion euros for adaptation from 2026 to 2030. Net-zero export finance reached about 376 billion dollars, up 58 percent.

props.label: Net-zero government export finance, up 58% year on year

beats.narration: The UK also backed the Presidency's 35 by 35 Global Electrification Pledge, and announced a UK–Nigeria low-methane partnership. Countries stepped up action on methane, forests and oceans.
Simon Stiell, the UN climate chief, acknowledged the frustration of delegates. He urged countries to learn lessons from Antalya, warning that the world cannot afford a repeat of this moment.

props.text: The world cannot afford a repeat of this moment.
props.attribution: Simon Stiell, UN Climate Change, 22 November 2026

beats.narration: The World Resources Institute called the result hollow. It said this was a failure of political leadership, not a failure of the Paris Agreement itself.

props.text: A failure of political leadership, not of the Paris Agreement.

beats.narration: Meanwhile, the Climate Action Tracker says 158 countries have submitted 2035 targets as of 6 November. Its verdict: they have failed to move the needle, and warming is heading for an irrecoverable overshoot of 1.5 degrees.

props.label: Countries submitted 2035 climate targets, as of 6 November 2026

beats.narration: Carbon Brief reports fossil CO2 may fall about 0.4 percent in 2026, driven by an oil drop and the Hormuz energy shock. That is not a policy success.

props.label: Expected fall in fossil CO2 emissions in 2026

beats.narration: Look at the details. Oil emissions down 1.9 percent explains most of it. Coal still edging up shows the underlying trend has not turned.
So what now? COP31 formally concluded on 22 November. Negotiations continue at COP32 in Ethiopia, and the successful items on finance and just transition still stand.
The takeaway: the headline deal collapsed, but the agreements on finance, just transition and electrification survive. Experts say the real test is whether leaders deliver at COP32.

props.text: The pact failed, but the work continues toward COP32.

accuracy.reason: Mostly faithful to the notes, but several claims are shaky: the Stiell quote is dated 22 Nov although the notes do not date it, "Experts say the real test is whether leaders deliver" is not in the notes, and the Climate Action Tracker 'irrecoverable overshoot' claim is conditional.

coverage.reason: Covers the COP31 collapse, the partial successes and the science, but has almost no major national announcements (US, EU, China, NDC specifics), no real expert forecasts of what comes next, and omits the US angle for a US viewer.

structure.reason: Clear chapters (what happened, what succeeded, reaction and science, what next) that build logically with one takeaway; beats 12-13 on emissions are slightly repetitive.

hook_ending.reason: The opener 'Two weeks of climate talks. Almost fifty hours of overtime. And still no deal.' is decent, but the ending is a summary-style takeaway with a vague 'real test' line.

tone.reason: Neutral, news-like and suitable for a general US audience.
